Part 1

How to use this book

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. This part sets your pace. A steady plan beats cramming, especially when the date is still open.

How to study it.

  1. Read it once, slowly, out loud.
  2. Pick one time each evening and keep it. The habit does half the work.
  3. Each night, do only what the plan says. Stop when the 20 minutes are up.

Watch for.

  • Reading the whole book in one sitting. It feels productive, but very little sticks.

Mindset. Slow and steady is a strength here. Panels reward calm, not speed.

Say it back. Can you say the study rule in one sentence? Every answer ends on leadership.

This edition runs on one list of eleven anchor stories. Every practice question points to one of them, and every story is a real one you can defend when the panel asks which bill, who disagreed and what happened next.

Learn the stories, not the sentences. For each one, know the turning point, the three things you personally did, the result, and what it says about how you lead. If you can tell it at lunch to a friend, you know it well enough.

THE STUDY RULE

Every answer ends on leadership. The panel is hiring a director, so after the result, say in one sentence what the story shows about how you lead people, partner with executives or protect the company.

Study plan while the date is open

When Focus How
Now to early December Opening, closing and Part 5, Know ComEd Say the opening and closing out loud every day. Record yourself once a week and listen for anything that sounds memorized.
First half of December Stories 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10 Tell each one out loud, then answer its follow-ups. Time each answer. Aim for two minutes.
Once the date is set All eleven stories and the decoder Run random-question drills from Part 11. Ten seconds to pick the story, then answer.
Two weeks out A mock panel Ask someone you trust outside your department to play the panel and push on follow-ups.
The week of ComEd news Check the items marked Check in Part 5, especially the ICC ruling on Grid Plan 2, the veto session outcome on data centers and the ComEd Four retrial.
The night before The day-of sheet only Nothing new. Read Part 4, rest, and trust the preparation.

Part 2

Your memory system

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. This is how a slow learner beats a fast one. Pulling an answer out of your head builds memory. Rereading only feels like it does.

How to study it.

  1. Learn the four Rs first. Read, Recall, Repeat, Rehearse.
  2. Walk the memory palace one room a night, eyes closed, out loud.
  3. Follow the review dots on the spacing calendar. Each dot is a five-minute recall, not a reread.

Watch for.

  • Skipping the recall step because it feels hard. That hard feeling is the learning happening.

Mindset. Forgetting is normal and expected. Each time you pull something back, it stays longer.

Say it back. Name the four Rs and the first three rooms of your palace without looking.

Knowing a story and finding it in four seconds while three people watch you are two different skills. This system builds both. It uses the methods with the strongest research behind them, retrieval practice, spacing, pictures and the memory palace, and pairs them with tools that do the scheduling for you.

START HERE, IN PLAIN WORDS

You only need three habits. Everything else in this part explains why they work.

  1. Learn the five-word chain. Every story has five keywords at the top, one for each STAR beat. Learn the chain and the story comes back.

  2. Picture the room. Every story lives in one room of your home with one picture. See the room and you know which story to tell.

  3. Do ten minutes of flashcards a day. The flashcard app decides what you review, so nothing fades.

The daily 20 minutes

  1. Flashcards, ten minutes.

  2. Walk the palace and say each five-word chain, three minutes.

  3. Tell one full story out loud and time it, three minutes.

  4. One random question from Part 11 using the story picker, four minutes.

Seven techniques and where they show up

Technique What it is Where you will see it
Retrieval practice Pulling an answer out of memory instead of rereading it. Every time you pull, the memory gets stronger. Close-the-book drills, the flashcard deck, the story picker
Spaced repetition Reviewing just before you would forget, at longer and longer gaps. The calendar in this part and the flashcard app
Dual coding Pairing words with a picture so you have two ways back to the memory. An infographic in every section and an image in every story
Memory palace Placing each story in a room along a route you already know. The palace map below and a room in every story
Chunking Shrinking a two-minute story to five keywords. The STAR chain at the top of every story
Hooks and acrostics A short phrase or first letters that unlock a list. Memory hooks in Know ComEd, the openers and the posting duties
Interleaving Mixing question types so you practice choosing the story, not just telling it. The story picker and random drills in Parts 11 and 12

Your memory palace, made simple

A memory palace is a mental filing system. You already know the rooms of your home by heart, so you use them as the index. One story goes in each room, always in the same order.

  1. Learn the order once. Porch, front door, living room, kitchen, dining room, hallway, stairs, den, office, garage, backyard.

  2. Put one picture in each room. The picture is a clue to the story. The table below explains each clue.

  3. In the interview, when you hear a question, ask yourself which room it belongs in. The picture brings the story.

# Room What you picture Why it points to the story
1 Front porch A round table sits on your porch with gas pipes for legs. A small pilot light burns on top of a law book stamped CRGA. The table is everyone you brought in early. The gas pipes are thermal networks. The pilot light is the pilot path that became law in CRGA.
2 Front door A former senator wedges a list in your front door. You point to a sign on the door that reads Same Door for Every Vendor, then call your boss. Every vendor uses the same front door, the vendor process. Calling your boss is reporting it up right away.
3 Living room A 2011 tour bus is parked in your living room, packed with legislators. A 2013 award plaque hangs over the fireplace. The 2011 tour you ran with district legislators for EIMA, and the award you received in 2013.
4 Kitchen A fiber cable boils over on the stove. The oven timer reads hours, not days. Three sticky notes on the fridge say What happens, Smallest fix, Who can change it. Broadband fiber boiling over is the crisis. The timer is the deadline. The notes are your three crisis questions.
5 Dining room Your seat at the table has a place card that reads Not Endorsing, and a small guardrail fence circles your plate. You have a seat at the table without endorsing the bill, and guardrails around what you can say.
6 Hallway A bill slides down the hallway past a closed door marked Experts. Now a big weekly calendar hangs on the wall. The bill slid past the experts because it never went to them. The calendar is the weekly tracker you built.
7 Staircase You reach the top of the stairs alone. The president is waiting and points back down. You go back and bring the team up with you. Leave no man behind. You go back and bring the team with you.
8 Den An expert in a lab coat argues with a legislator. You step between them holding two cards, one says Value and one says Behavior. Value the expert, correct the behavior.
9 Home office A scale sits on your desk. One side holds a thick voting record, the other a small storm cloud. The record wins. The voting record outweighs one stormy meeting.
10 Garage You hold a ladder steady while a former Senate staffer climbs up to a sign that reads Manager. You held the ladder while she climbed to manager.
11 Backyard A fence marked Statute surrounds the garden. The ICC is the gardener tending the plants inside. The law sets the fence. The ICC tends the details inside it.

If your home has a different layout, keep the order and change the room names. The order matters more than the rooms.

Spaced review calendar

The plan gets you interview-ready by December 12. If the interview comes later, the review dots keep everything fresh without cramming. Each dot is a five-minute recall, not a reread.

  • Learn it means read the story once, picture the room, then tell it out loud twice.

  • A review means cover the page, say the five-word chain, then tell the story. Check what you missed.

  • Forty-eight hours out, run one full mock panel. After that, only the day-of sheet.

Tools that make it stick

Tool Use it for How
Anki with FSRS Flashcards on a schedule that learns your memory Free on computers and Android, paid on iPhone. Import the ComEd flashcard file that came with this book, turn on FSRS in the deck options, and do ten minutes a day.
Quizlet The same cards in a simpler app Import the same flashcard file if you prefer Quizlet.
Claude voice mode A mock panel that asks follow-ups Use the prompt below, answer out loud, and ask for a score after each answer.

MOCK PANEL PROMPT FOR CLAUDE VOICE MODE

Act as a three-person ComEd hiring panel for the Director of Government and Legislative Affairs role. Ask me one behavioral question at a time. After I answer, ask two follow-ups that test my personal role and the result. Then score me on clarity, ownership, leadership and length, and tell me the one thing to fix. Mix in questions about ComEd’s grid plan, data centers and affordability.

Part 3

Competencies and the questions that test them

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. The panel scores you on competencies, not stories. This map tells you which story proves which strength.

How to study it.

  1. Learn the leadership thread first. No surprises, One voice, Right way, Stronger team.
  2. Take three competencies a night and say which story proves each one.
  3. Read the Exelon words table once a week so their language feels natural in your mouth.

Watch for.

  • Trying to memorize the whole table. You only need the link from each competency to a story.

Mindset. You have done this work for eighteen years. This part just gives it the names the panel uses.

Say it back. Say the four thread words, and one story that proves each.

Every behavioral question tests one competency. If you can name the competency in the first few seconds, you know which story to tell and what the panel needs to hear at the end. This map ties each competency to the questions you are likely to hear and to your best stories. The numbers in the table match the rows in the chart.

MEMORY HOOK

Name it before you answer. The competency tells you which story to tell and how to end it.

# Competency What the panel is really asking Questions sound like Story End on this point
1 Legislative strategy Can you set direction on a major bill, not just react to it? Develop a strategy, anticipate an issue, reposition when politics change, most significant accomplishment 1, then 11 I shaped the outcome, not just our position.
2 Leading without authority Can you move people who do not report to you? Align departments, lead an initiative with people outside your team, explain investment and bills 3, then 11 I gave people a reason to care and a clear decision.
3 Executive communication Will you tell executives the truth, early and briefly? Bad news to leadership, briefing when things are fluid, turning Springfield intelligence into advice 9, then 5 No surprises. Facts first, then a recommendation.
4 Crisis and risk judgment Do you stay organized when time is short and facts are missing? Late-session amendment, little time to act, incomplete information, a bad precedent 4, then 5 Speed with a plan, and decisions at the right level.
5 Integrity and compliance Will you protect the company when the pressure comes? Pressure against ethics rules, a request you could not grant, keeping lobbyists in line 2 Same rules for everyone, reported up right away.
6 Coalitions and stakeholders Can you build support beyond the usual allies? Coalition for a utility issue, disagreement with an advocate, allies split, a better messenger 1, then 4 Aligned interests and the right messenger.
7 Developing people Will you grow a team, not just manage one? Someone you developed, mentoring, building a bench, your philosophy 10, then 7 The people around me get better.
8 Accountability and conflict Can you correct someone and keep the relationship? Holding someone accountable, a difficult person, correcting someone senior 8, then 9 Private, specific, tied to impact, followed up.
9 Self-awareness and learning Do you own your mistakes and change? A time you failed, a policy loss, feedback that changed you, weaknesses 6, then 7 I owned it and changed the process.
10 Process and value creation Do you leave systems better than you found them? Improving a process, leading change, building consistency across a team 6, then the change answer in Part 8 One fix became a system the team uses.
11 Utility and policy know-how Do you understand the business behind the bill? Statute or ICC, regulatory flexibility, ComEd’s grid plan, data centers, affordability 11, then 3 and Part 5 The right detail in the right venue.
12 Political and community presence Can you represent the company and its officers well? PAC, events and fundraising, trade associations, storms, the Governor’s office Part 10, then 2 Inside the rules, every time.
13 Motivation and fit Why you, why ComEd, why now? Tell me about yourself, why ComEd, why now, why not stay Part 8 Ready to lead, at the right company, at the right time.

Your leadership thread

Every answer should sound like it came from the same leader. These four themes run through your stories, your scripts and your closing. When you finish an answer, land on one of them.

MEMORY HOOK

No surprises, One voice, Right way, Stronger team.

Theme What it sounds like Where you prove it
No surprises Executives hear it from me first, good news or bad, with a recommendation attached. Stories 4, 5 and 9
One voice I align the experts inside the company before we speak outside it. Stories 1, 3 and 11
Right way Same rules for everyone, every time, with compliance in the room early. Story 2 and the PAC answer in Part 10
Stronger team I develop people, share what I know and hold people to a clear standard. Stories 7, 8 and 10

Work together to solve problems I bring legal, regulatory, operations and executives to one company position. One voice
Trust, respect and a high-performance culture Executives hear it from me first, and I hold the team to a clear standard. No surprises, Stronger team
Full compliance with all statutes governing external relationships Same rules for everyone, every time, with compliance in the room early. Right way
People can grow, develop new skills and build careers One way I measure myself is the talent I leave behind. Stronger team
Improving how we work I built a weekly bill tracker and an expert routing database that the team uses. Stronger team
Presentations at statewide forums, data and analyses for policymakers I turn complicated policy into plain language for members and executives. One voice

The day-of sheet

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. This is the one page you read in the parking lot. It has to feel familiar long before that day.

How to study it.

  1. Read it at the end of every session, even nights you study something else.
  2. Once a week, try to write it from memory, then compare.

Watch for.

  • Adding notes until it spills onto a second page. Keep it to one page.

Mindset. The sheet is a reminder, not a script. You already know what is on it.

Say it back. Without looking, list the five opener beats and your three questions for the panel.

THREE QUESTIONS TO ASK THE PANEL SUCCESS, SPEED, MAGIC WAND

  • What does success look like in this role? If we are sitting together a year from now, what would I have done to earn a strong review?

  • How does your team like to collaborate, especially when things move fast or priorities shift?

  • If you could wave a magic wand, what is the one challenge your team faces today that you would solve overnight?

Part 5

Know ComEd

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. This shows you did your homework and can talk about their world, not just Ameren's.

How to study it.

  1. One section a night. Learn the memory hook first, then the baseline script, then the Ameren contrast.
  2. Say each script out loud twice. The second time, look away from the page.
  3. Pick two or three numbers you can say with confidence. Leave the rest on the page.

Watch for.

  • Guessing a figure in the room. Say roughly, or go straight to the point the number makes.
  • Criticizing ComEd's past. Acknowledge it in one sentence, then talk about what you would build.

Mindset. Nobody expects you to know ComEd like an insider. They expect you to be curious and prepared, and you will be.

Say it back. Say Big Grids Demand Every Storm Survived, and what each word stands for.

Each section ends with a baseline script, what you would say in 30 to 45 seconds if the panel asks about it.

A director is expected to talk about ComEd’s business the way an executive would, not only its politics. This part is your briefing book. Facts are current as of late November 2026. Items marked Check may change before your interview, so look them up the week you go in.

ComEd at a glance

MEMORY HOOK

4, 70, 11,400, 24. Four million customers, 70 percent of the state, 11,400 square miles, a 24 gigawatt peak.

Item What to know
Who they are The largest electric utility in Illinois and the largest of Exelon’s utilities. Headquartered in Chicago. A wires company. ComEd delivers power but does not own power plants.
Customers More than 4 million, about 70 percent of the state’s population.
Territory About 11,400 square miles of northern Illinois. From the Wisconsin line south to roughly Iroquois County and Pontiac, and from the Iowa border to the Indiana border, including the Chicago metro area, Rockford, Joliet and DeKalb.
The grid More than 90,000 miles of power lines. All-time system peak just under 24,000 MW.
Markets and regulators ComEd sits in PJM. Capacity costs from PJM auctions pass through to customers with no markup. The ICC regulates distribution and the grid plan. FERC regulates transmission.
Leadership Gil Quiniones, President and CEO. David Perez, Executive Vice President and COO. Calvin Butler leads parent company Exelon.
Political geography With about 70 percent of Illinoisans living in ComEd territory, most members of the General Assembly have ComEd customers as constituents.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

ComEd is the largest utility in Illinois. It serves more than four million customers, about 70 percent of the state’s people, across 11,400 square miles of northern Illinois. It is a wires company in PJM, so capacity prices set at PJM show up on customers’ bills even though ComEd does not set them. For a GR director that means two things. Nearly every member of the General Assembly has ComEd customers, so every member is a stakeholder. And we have to help members see the difference between what ComEd controls and what it does not, without sounding like we are making excuses.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • 1.2 million electric and about 816,000 natural gas customers.

  • 43,700 square miles, about three-quarters of the state’s land, more than 1,200 communities.

  • MISO, not PJM. Electric and gas delivery, not electric only.

Contrast script. I come from the other side of the map. Ameren Illinois covers about three-quarters of the state’s land with 1.2 million electric customers and another 816,000 on gas, spread across more than 1,200 communities in MISO. So I know downstate and rural members, and I know what it takes to bring them along on a statewide bill.

Financial snapshot

MEMORY HOOK

22, 41, 16, 8.9. A $22.4 billion rate base, Exelon’s $41.7 billion plan, transmission growing 16 percent a year, an 8.905 percent return.

Item What to know
Rate base $22.4 billion in 2025, the largest in the Exelon family.
Earnings trend Third quarter 2026 net income of $406 million, up from $373 million a year earlier, driven by growth in distribution and transmission rate base.
Parent capital plan Exelon projects $41.7 billion of capital spending from 2026 through 2029 and about 7.9 percent annual rate base growth.
Where the growth is Transmission. Exelon expects its transmission rate base to grow about 16 percent a year through 2029, with another $12 to $17 billion of transmission opportunity over the next decade.
How ComEd earns Distribution earnings are decoupled from weather and usage. Since CEJA, ComEd earns through a multi-year rate plan tied to an ICC-approved grid plan, with yearly reconciliations and performance metrics. The current plan’s authorized return on equity is 8.905 percent.
Customer bills The average residential bill was about $106 a month in early 2026. ComEd reports its residential rate about 22 percent below the average of the ten largest US metro areas.

WHY IT MATTERS TO GR

Almost every dollar of ComEd’s growth runs through a legislative or regulatory decision. The grid plan, the rate plan, transmission policy and data center rules all shape the business plan. That makes Government Relations part of how the company protects its earnings and its customers at the same time.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

ComEd is the largest part of Exelon, with about $22 billion in rate base, and Exelon plans about $41.7 billion of investment through 2029, much of it in transmission. ComEd earns through a multi-year rate plan tied to an approved grid plan, with an authorized return of about 8.9 percent. So nearly every dollar of growth runs through Springfield or the ICC. As director, I would make sure the executive team sees GR as part of protecting that plan, and that legislators see what customers get for every dollar.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • Ameren plans $31.8 billion of investment from 2026 through 2030, with rate base growing about 10.6 percent a year.

  • Ameren Illinois’ authorized return under its grid plan is 8.715 percent, compared with ComEd’s 8.905 percent.

  • Ameren Illinois also runs a regulated gas business, which received a $79 million rate increase in 2025.

Contrast script. The model is the same at Ameren Illinois. A multi-year plan, yearly reconciliations and an ICC-approved return, ours at 8.715 percent. The difference is scale and mix. Ameren Illinois also runs a gas business, so I am used to defending investment on two fronts at once.

The grid plans

MEMORY HOOK

Rejected, Approved, Trimmed, Filed, Ruled, Rates, Runs. One word for each milestone, in order.

  • Grid Plan 1, 2024 to 2027. The ICC rejected ComEd’s first plan in December 2023 for falling short of CEJA’s affordability and environmental justice standards. The refiled plan was approved in December 2024 with about 25 percent less spending than proposed and a $606 million rate increase over four years, roughly 11 percent below the request.

  • Yearly reconciliations. The ICC now checks actual spending against the plan every year. In December 2025 it cut $25.4 million from a $268.5 million request, mostly costs tied to the troubled 2024 billing system rollout, and removed performance incentives connected to it.

  • Grid Plan 2, 2028 to 2031. Filed January 16, 2026, at about $15.3 billion. It includes new substations, added capacity at more than 70 existing substations, more than a third of spending for reliability, and upgrades for electric vehicles, electric heat, data centers and renewables. ComEd projects bills rising about $2.50 to $3 a month starting in 2028. The Citizens Utility Board called it bloated and expensive, and the Attorney General and environmental groups are also intervening.

  • What comes next. The ICC decision on Grid Plan 2 is expected in December 2026, and ComEd files its next rate plan in January 2027. Your interview may land in the middle of both.

CHECK

Whether the ICC has ruled on Grid Plan 2, and how much it cut.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

Both big utilities had their first grid plans sent back in 2023. ComEd’s refiled plan was approved in December 2024 with a $606 million increase over four years. The ICC now checks spending every year, and in 2025 it cut about $25 million, mostly billing system costs. The second plan, about $15.3 billion for 2028 through 2031, gets a ruling in December, and the rate filing follows in January. As director, my job would be making sure members understand what that investment buys before the rate case lands in their districts.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • The first Ameren Illinois grid plan was also rejected in December 2023.

  • The refiled plan was approved in December 2024 at about $309 million over four years.

  • Ameren appealed the December 2025 reconciliation order in March 2026.

  • Its second grid plan for 2028 through 2031 was filed in early 2026.

Contrast script. I have lived this process on the Ameren side. Our first plan was also sent back, the refiled plan was approved, and I have done legislator outreach on our grid plan. The lesson is the same at both companies. Explain the value early, in district terms, before the bill headlines show up.

The 10 to 20 year outlook

MEMORY HOOK

Picture the curve. Small today, steep after 2028, about 10,800 MW by 2035, and possibly double the peak by 2040. Then add the wildcard, weather.

  • Demand could double. ComEd received about 30,000 MW of data center requests over three years. Serving the full pipeline would more than double a system peak that took 120 years to build, most likely arriving in stages through 2040 to 2045.

  • PJM forecast. PJM’s 2026 forecast adds about 885 MW of large load in the ComEd zone in 2026, growing to roughly 10,800 MW by 2035. Across PJM, summer peak demand is projected to climb from 160 GW in 2025 to 253 GW by 2046, and ComEd is one of four zones with the largest data center pipelines.

  • Transmission build-out. Transmission is the biggest capital driver for the decade, and it is regulated at FERC rather than the ICC.

  • Supply and reliability. PJM capacity is tight. Exelon has argued for utility-owned generation and storage as a backstop for reliability risks as early as 2028. In Illinois that would take legislation, so expect a major fight.

  • Affordability pressure. Under the grid plan filing, electricity’s share of the average household’s income rises from 1.23 percent in 2026 to 1.41 percent in 2028 and keeps climbing through 2031. CEJA’s benchmark is 3 percent, or 6 percent for electric heat.

  • Policy calendar. CRGA implementation, including storage, virtual power plants and new state resource planning. The carbon mitigation credit program runs through 2027, so what follows it becomes a live question. The nuclear moratorium is lifted, and the state is reassessing coal and gas retirement deadlines.

  • Weather. 2026 was ComEd’s most severe storm season on record, with 19 major storms, 59 tornadoes and about 2.4 million customer interruptions. A ComEd and Argonne study found severe rainfall events could nearly double in the next 15 years. Resilience spending and storm cost recovery will grow.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

The next twenty years are about load growth and who pays for it. Data center requests could more than double ComEd’s peak by around 2040, which means more transmission, tighter supply in PJM and steady pressure on bills. Add a record storm year and the end of the carbon credit program in 2027, and the agenda writes itself. As director, I would want ComEd setting the terms of that debate. Large loads paying their own way, a clear reliability case, and a voice in what replaces the carbon credits, instead of reacting to someone else’s bill.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • MISO’s capacity shortage pushed Ameren Illinois’ summer 2025 supply price from about 8 to about 12 cents per kilowatt-hour.

  • Downstate bills rose roughly 18 to 22 percent that summer.

  • The future of the gas system is a live question at the ICC.

  • CRGA’s battery storage is projected to save Ameren customers more per month than ComEd customers by 2031.

Contrast script. Downstate, the pressure looks different. MISO’s capacity shortage pushed Ameren Illinois’ summer supply price up by about half in 2025, and the future of the gas system is a live question at the ICC. Both companies face the same core issue, affordability during growth. I have worked that issue in both markets.

What is working well

MEMORY HOOK

The Five Rs. Reliability, Rates, Relief, Ring-fenced data center costs, Robust finances.

  • Reliability. ComEd ranked first among peer utilities in 2025 benchmarking and was top decile on both outage frequency and duration. Reliability has improved more than 57 percent since smart grid work began in 2012, avoiding nearly 24.7 million customer interruptions and more than $4.3 billion in outage costs.

  • Rates. Residential, commercial and industrial rates run well below large-metro averages.

  • Relief. CEJA’s carbon mitigation credits have returned more than $1.8 billion to ComEd customers since 2022, including about $580 million in the first quarter of 2026. A Low-Income Discount program launched in January 2026, ComEd reported more than $100 million in customer relief in 2025, and new time-of-day rates help customers save.

  • Ring-fenced data center costs. In January 2026 ComEd signed agreements with eight large-load customers seeking more than 6.5 GW. They require financial commitments for transmission, which ComEd says keeps other customers from paying more than $2 billion over a decade. The ICC also approved higher deposits for large-load developers in March 2026.

  • Robust finances. Steady earnings growth, a large capital plan and a parent with strong investment-grade credit.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

ComEd has real strengths to build on. It led its peers in reliability in 2025, its rates are below big-city averages, customers have received more than $1.8 billion in carbon credits since 2022, and its large-load agreements protect other customers from data center costs. Good GR puts those facts in front of members before the critics define the company. As director, I would make sure every member knows what ComEd delivers in their district.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • Ameren Illinois reports reliability up about 23 percent and more than 6.5 million outages prevented.

  • In 2025, businesses in its Illinois territory created more than 1,450 jobs and invested $2 billion.

  • CRGA roughly doubles Ameren’s energy efficiency programs.

Contrast script. Ameren Illinois tells a similar story downstate. Reliability is up about 23 percent with more than 6.5 million outages prevented, and in 2025 businesses in its territory created more than 1,450 jobs and invested $2 billion. In both places, reliability and economic development are the facts that win over skeptical members.

Looming problems

MEMORY HOOK

Big Grids Demand Every Storm Survived. Bills, Grid Plan 2, Data centers, Execution, Storms, Scandal tail.

  • Bills. Record PJM capacity prices added about $10.60 a month to the average residential bill in summer 2025 and another $2 to $3 in summer 2026, on top of delivery increases. Affordability is the dominant political issue in energy.

  • Grid Plan 2 cost. A $15.3 billion plan lands while customers are already angry about bills, and the main consumer advocates are opposing it.

  • Data center politics. The POWER Act, which would make large data centers bring their own clean energy and disclose energy and water use, stalled in spring and is back in the veto session with a December 3 deadline. In June 2026 the Governor paused new state tax incentives for data centers. The question of who pays is not settled.

  • Execution. The 2024 billing system launch left customers unable to see or pay bills, disrupted community solar billing for months and cost ComEd in the 2025 reconciliation. The ICC is applying tougher, performance-based scrutiny.

  • Storms. A record storm year raises cost recovery and resilience questions just as affordability is under pressure.

  • The scandal’s long tail. A possible February 2027 retrial for two of the ComEd Four keeps the history in the news.

CHECK

Whether the POWER Act or another data center bill passed in the veto session, and what it requires of utilities.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

The pressure points are bills, the cost of the new grid plan, who pays for data centers, execution problems like the billing system, storm costs and the long tail of the scandal. Affordability ties them together. As director, I would start there, because if ComEd is not leading on affordability, someone else will write that bill for us.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • Bills driven by MISO capacity prices.

  • Gas affordability and the future of the gas system.

  • The cost of serving a large rural territory.

  • No corruption history or compliance agreement.

Contrast script. Ameren Illinois faces the same affordability squeeze from a different direction, MISO capacity prices, gas costs and the expense of serving a large rural territory. What Ameren does not carry is a corruption history. That is why I would lead with process and transparency at ComEd from day one.

Reputation, political and business

MEMORY HOOK

Strong wires, rebuilding trust. Operations earn respect. Politics still has to be earned back.

  • In Springfield, trust is still being rebuilt. After the 2020 deferred prosecution agreement and $200 million federal fine, the ICC fined ComEd another $38 million in 2022. CEJA replaced formula rates with performance-based grid and rate plans, and the ICC is enforcing them.

  • Consumer advocates are adversarial and quotable. CUB challenges nearly every major filing. Environmental groups are focused on data centers. Building trades labor is often an ally on infrastructure and data center growth.

  • The administration. Governor Pritzker and ComEd have lined up on pressing PJM to rein in capacity prices, while the Governor presses data centers to pay their own way.

  • With investors and peers, ComEd is seen as a reliable, well-run delivery utility with strong growth ahead.

  • With customers, rising bills and the billing system problems dominate. Reliability is a real strength that customers rarely notice.

HOW TO TALK ABOUT REPUTATION

Be balanced and forward-looking. ComEd’s operational reputation is strong. Its political reputation is still being rebuilt, and affordability is the pressure point. GR earns credibility back by being the most reliable source of facts in the building and by bringing workable solutions.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

Operationally, ComEd is respected. Investors and peers see a reliable, well-run utility. Politically, trust is still being rebuilt, consumer advocates challenge nearly every filing, and customers feel the bills. Trust comes back through consistency. As director, I would want our team known as the most reliable source of facts in the building, the people who bring workable solutions, and a team that follows the rules every time.

AMEREN ILLINOIS CONTRAST

  • CUB and the ICC press Ameren Illinois hard on affordability too.

  • The ICC rejected its first grid plan as well.

  • It does not operate under a compliance agreement, and its relationships downstate are built on long tenure.

Contrast script. Ameren Illinois gets the same tough questions on affordability from CUB and the ICC, but it does not carry a scandal. I have seen what a clean reputation is worth in Springfield. It gets you a hearing. My job at ComEd would be to keep earning that hearing.

The history the panel lives with

MEMORY HOOK

2011 to 2019, $200 million, retrial in 2027. Know it, never lead with it.

  • In July 2020 ComEd entered a deferred prosecution agreement and paid a $200 million fine. It admitted arranging jobs, vendor subcontracts and payments for associates of then House Speaker Michael Madigan from 2011 to 2019 to influence legislation.

  • The agreement required ComEd to strengthen its compliance program and report annually on it. Compliance is part of how that team works every day.

  • The scheme began in 2011, the same year EIMA passed. That is why EIMA is no longer your headline story.

  • In 2026 a federal appeals court ordered a new trial for former ComEd CEO Anne Pramaggiore and lobbyist Mike McClain, and a judge floated a February 2027 retrial date.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

Only if they ask. I know the history, and I know ComEd has rebuilt its compliance program since 2020. My approach has always been to do this work in the open and inside the rules, and that is how I would lead here.

Will EIMA and the senator story create a difficult conversation?

MEMORY HOOK

Senator up front, EIMA in the back. The ethics story leads. EIMA supports.

The senator story is low risk and high reward. It is close to the mirror image of what ComEd admitted, and it shows the panel exactly the judgment they need in this seat. Tell it plainly, do not name the senator, and do not draw the comparison yourself. Let them make it.

EIMA carries moderate risk, so it moves out of the headline spot. Your part was honest district work, and you have an award for it. But to this panel, EIMA as your greatest accomplishment invites the wrong conversation. Your lead accomplishment is now thermal energy networks to CRGA, which is recent, ends in a law ComEd is implementing, and shows you turning opposition into policy. EIMA stays as your leading-without-authority story, with a calm, prepared answer if the history comes up.

ComEd and Ameren Illinois side by side

MEMORY HOOK

Same rules, different map. Same laws, same ICC process, same General Assembly. Different scale, market and politics.

ComEd Ameren Illinois
Region Northern Illinois, including Chicago and the collar counties Central and southern Illinois
Customers More than 4 million electric 1.2 million electric and about 816,000 natural gas
Territory About 11,400 square miles, about 70 percent of the state’s people 43,700 square miles, about three-quarters of the state’s land, 1,200 communities

Parent company Exelon, Chicago Ameren Corporation, St. Louis

HOW TO USE THE COMPARISON

  • What carries over. CEJA and CRGA, the ICC grid plan and reconciliation process, the same legislature and many of the same advocates.

  • What is new for you. Four times the customers, PJM instead of MISO, electric only, Chicago politics and ComEd’s history.

  • Your edge. You know how downstate members see energy. ComEd needs their votes too.

BASELINE SCRIPT, SAY IT LIKE THIS

Ameren Illinois covers about three-quarters of the state’s land, and ComEd serves about 70 percent of its people. We work under the same laws, CEJA and now CRGA, the same ICC grid plan process and the same General Assembly. What is different is scale, PJM instead of MISO, electric only, and Chicago politics. I know the framework from the inside, and I know how downstate members see energy, which helps when ComEd needs votes beyond the city and the suburbs.

ComEd questions the panel may ask

ComEd has been through a lot in Springfield. How would you lead Government Relations here?

HOOK Open, same rules, compliance early, no surprises.

I would lead it the way I have always worked, in the open and inside the rules. Everyone on the team knows the rules and applies them the same way for every legislator. Compliance is in the room early, not after the fact. And leadership hears from me first, good news or bad. Credibility in Springfield comes from doing it the right way every time, and from being the team that brings workable solutions.

What do you see as the biggest legislative challenge facing ComEd in the next two years?

HOOK Affordability. Supply, large loads pay, show the value.

Affordability, and everything that touches it. Bills went up because of capacity prices ComEd does not control, the second grid plan is in front of the ICC, and data centers are raising the question of who pays. I would want ComEd seen as part of the answer. Pressing PJM on supply, making sure large loads pay their own way, and showing members exactly what customers get for every grid dollar. If we are not leading on affordability, someone else will write that bill for us.

What do you know about our grid plan?

HOOK Sent back, approved, $15.3B pending, December ruling.

The first plan was sent back in 2023 and approved after a refiling in 2024. The second plan, about $15.3 billion for 2028 through 2031, is in front of the ICC now, with a decision expected in December and a rate filing in January. The investment is about reliability and getting ready for load growth, and the challenge is explaining that to members whose constituents are already upset about bills. I have done that kind of outreach on Ameren’s grid plan.

How would you approach the data center debate?

HOOK Pay their own way, honest broker, workable bill.

Start from where ComEd already is. The large-load agreements and higher deposits protect other customers from paying for speculative projects. I would support growth that pays its own way, make ComEd the honest broker on what the grid can handle and when, and work with labor, economic development leaders and the advocates so whatever passes is something the utility can actually implement.

You are coming from Ameren. What is different about ComEd?

HOOK Scale, PJM, politics. Same framework. Downstate votes.

Scale, PJM instead of MISO, and the politics. Most of the General Assembly represents ComEd customers, and Chicago’s issues are different from downstate’s. What is the same is the framework. CEJA, the ICC grid plan process and now CRGA. I have worked inside that framework for years, and I bring an understanding of how downstate members think about energy, which matters when you need 60 and 30 votes.

Rules for the room. Do not raise the scandal first. Do not dodge it if asked. Never criticize people by name. Talk about how you would lead, not about what others did.

Part 6

The HR phone screen

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. This call is the gate. The recruiter is checking fit, basics and pay, not deep stories.

How to study it.

  1. Practice each answer at 30 to 60 seconds. Use a timer on your phone.
  2. Say your salary answer out loud until it sounds normal to you.
  3. Say your notice line, two to four weeks, and your registered lobbyist line until they come easily.

Watch for.

  • Going too deep. Long stories belong with the panel.
  • Naming a number before they do. The posted range lets you anchor on their numbers.

Mindset. Friendly and brief. Smile while you talk. It comes through on the phone.

Say it back. Say your salary answer and your why ComEd answer without looking.

The phone screen is a short call, usually 20 to 30 minutes, with a recruiter or HR partner. Their job is to confirm you meet the basics, hear your story, check salary and logistics, and decide whether to send you to the panel. They are not grading STAR depth. Keep answers to 30 to 60 seconds, warm and specific, and offer to give the panel the full story.

MEMORY HOOK

Short, warm, specific. Headline first, one proof point, then stop. Smile while you talk. They can hear it.

The recruiter is checking Make sure they hear
Minimum qualifications Eighteen years in Illinois government relations, a staff of seven for seven years, five years in HR
Fit with the posting You lead company positions on state legislation, align experts, brief executives and direct contract lobbyists
Motivation Ready to lead, ComEd has been on your list for years, Ameren has few director seats
Logistics Open to relocating, comfortable with Springfield travel and storm hours
Compensation You know the posted range and where you fit in it
Red flags No criticism of Ameren, nothing confidential, no rambling

Before the call

  • Quiet room, phone charged, and stand up. Your voice carries more energy standing.

  • Have the posting, the day-of sheet and this part open in front of you.

  • Write your target base pay on a sticky note. The posted range is $164,800 to $226,600, plus bonus and long-term incentive.

  • Have your calendar open so you can schedule the panel on the spot.

  • Know the name of the ComEd team member who encouraged you to apply.

Background and fit

MEMORY HOOK

Who, Why, Leave, Know, Heard. One word per question, in order.

Walk me through your background.

HOOK Decision, eighteen years, roots, three things.

Sure. I’m a Senior Government Relations Representative at Ameren Illinois, and I’ve been in Government Relations for eighteen years. The short version is that I turn policy fights into decisions the company can stand behind, and then I win support for them in Springfield. Today I’m my department’s lead on data center, battery storage and decarbonization bills, and I work closely with legal, regulatory, operations and our executives to get to one company position. Before Government Relations, I ran a health and welfare plan with a staff of seven and a board of trustees, and I spent five years in Ameren’s HR group, including two mergers and the company’s first shared services model. So I bring Springfield, the business behind the bill and real people leadership, and I’d love to bring that to ComEd.

What interests you about this role?

HOOK Lead, same agenda, short list.

Three things. First, it’s a leadership role, leading the team and the company’s position on every state issue, and that’s the step I’m ready for. Second, ComEd’s agenda is the one I already work on, data centers, affordability, CRGA and grid planning. And third, ComEd has been on my short list for years, so when this opened, it felt like the right time.

Why are you looking to leave Ameren?

HOOK Not running. Few seats. Ready to lead.

I’m not running from anything. I’ve had a great run at Ameren and a real seat at the table with senior leaders. Government Relations is a small function, and director roles don’t open often. I’m ready to lead with the title, and I’d rather do that at a company I’ve respected for a long time.

What do you know about ComEd?

HOOK 4 million, reliability, four big issues.

ComEd serves more than four million customers, about 70 percent of the state, and it’s the largest part of Exelon. Operationally it’s strong. It led its peers in reliability last year. The big issues right now are affordability with PJM capacity costs, data center growth and who pays for it, the second grid plan in front of the ICC, and implementing CRGA. Those are the same issues I work on every day from the Ameren side.

How did you hear about the position?

HOOK Name the person, then the long interest.

[Name] on the Government and Legislative Affairs team reached out and encouraged me to apply. I’ve followed ComEd for a long time, so I was glad to.

Qualifications the recruiter must confirm

MEMORY HOOK

Years, People, Style, Executives, Win, Ethics. One word per question, in order.

The role calls for at least 12 years in the legislative arena. Tell me about yours.

HOOK Eighteen years, three big laws, a full bill portfolio.

I have eighteen years in Illinois government relations, working the General Assembly, the executive branch and the ICC. I’ve worked the major energy laws of that period, EIMA, CEJA and CRGA, and each session I manage a portfolio of bills from tracking, to expert review, to a company position, to advocacy.

The posting asks for five years of supervisory experience. Tell me about that.

HOOK Seven, seven, five, plus the hard kind.

Yes. I ran Southwest Benefit Program for seven years with a staff of seven, plus our outside counsel and accountants, and I reported to a board of trustees. At Ameren I spent five years in HR advising managers on discipline, terminations, succession and labor relations, and supporting two merger integrations. And in Government Relations I train new team members on our processes and ethics, guide contract lobbyists and lead cross-functional teams on my issues. I’m ready to have a GR team on my own org chart.

How would you describe your leadership style?

HOOK Clear, collaborative, no surprises.

Clear and collaborative. I set the goal and the deadline up front, bring the right people in early and let the experts own their piece. When the clock is running in session, I get more directive. And I don’t surprise my leaders. They hear from me first, good news or bad, with a recommendation attached.

What is your experience working with senior executives?

HOOK Changed, means, decide.

A big part of my job is turning what’s happening in Springfield into something executives can act on. I do status reports, strategy calls and end-of-session reports, and in HR I worked with senior leaders on two mergers, the first shared services model, and executive pay and performance modeling. I keep it short. What changed, what it means and what we need to decide.

Tell me about a recent accomplishment.

HOOK Thermal networks, tabled, then CRGA.

Thermal energy networks. In 2025 a decarbonization bill came in that we couldn’t live with as written. I set our internal strategy, we moved from opposing it to offering a pilot path, the bill was tabled, and a workable version became law in CRGA. I’d be glad to walk the panel through it.

How do you approach ethics and compliance in lobbying?

HOOK Same rules, report up, audited.

Same rules for everyone, every time. I follow the state ethics rules and report out, a third-party auditor reviews our work twice a year, and our legal team reinforces it. I’ve been tested on that, when someone with influence pushed for something we couldn’t do, and I’m glad to share that example with the panel.

Logistics

Move, Travel, Pay, Start, Others, Obligations, Registered. One word per question, in order.

Yes. I’m ready to relocate to the Chicago area, and the hybrid schedule works well for me.

None at all. I’m in Springfield throughout session now, and I already work with our storm response team, including keeping legislators updated during outages. At this stage of life my schedule is my own.

I’m being selective. ComEd is my focus right now.

I don’t have a non-compete. I do take confidentiality seriously. I won’t bring anything confidential from Ameren, and I’d expect ComEd to hold me to that.

Yes, I’m registered with the Illinois Secretary of State and my filings are current.

SALARY COACHING

  • The range is posted. Base pay of $164,800 to $226,600, an annual bonus of 30 percent for eligible positions, and $50,000 a year in long-term incentive. You do not need to ask for it. Confirm it and anchor in the upper half.

  • The midpoint is $195,700. Your eighteen years and the scope of the role justify a target above it. Pick your number before the call and write it down.

  • You do not have to share your current pay. Illinois law bars employers from asking about salary history. If it comes up, steer back to the posted range and the value you bring.

  • Talk total package, not just base. Bonus, long-term incentive, 401(k), relocation and start date are all part of the conversation.

  • Say your number and stop talking. No apologies, no explaining.

Your career path

MEMORY HOOK

Fund, HR, GR, Today. Same title. MBA.

Walk me through your resume.

HOOK Fund, HR, GR, Today.

I started as Program Director of a Taft-Hartley health benefit program covering about 25,000 union members in five states. I ran a staff of seven, managed our lawyers, accountants and administrators, and worked for a board of trustees. You have held the same title since 2008. Why?

HOOK Small function, family first, scope grew.

Two honest reasons. Earlier in my career I chose roles that fit what my family needed, and Government Relations is a small function where leadership seats rarely open. What grew was my scope. More than you might think. Healthcare and utilities are both heavily regulated, and the core tension in both is cost versus access. Here it is affordability versus reliability. The Executive MBA gave me the finance, strategy and leadership tools, and I use them every time I weigh whether customers are paying a fair cost for something that lasts, without putting the business at unnecessary risk.

Your Government Relations work

MEMORY HOOK

Lead, Sixty, Router, Informed, Governor, PAC, National.

What does leading the department’s work on data centers, storage and decarbonization look like day to day?

HOOK Point person, one team, one position.

I am Government Relations’ point person on those issues. I guide a cross-functional team of business leaders and experts from the internal position, through communications, to advocacy. On data centers I coordinate with Economic Development and our Clean Energy Transition team, prepare bill analyses for House and Senate hearings and keep a data center legislation knowledge center so the whole team stays current as bills move.

How do you manage 60 bills a session?

HOOK Track, route, decide, brief.

With a system. Every assigned bill goes on a weekly tracker. Each one is routed to the right experts, I work with the responsible executive to reach a position before committee, and leadership gets intelligence briefings, written analyses and risk assessments as bills move. The goal is that nothing important reaches a committee without a company position behind it.

Tell us about the SME routing tool.

HOOK 109 topics, 25 sections, right expert fast.

It is a tool I built that matches any bill or issue to the right leader, department or team. It covers about 109 topics across 25 sections of an electric and gas utility. Before it, routing depended on who you happened to know. Now a bill reaches the right experts quickly, and we can settle positions before committee action. It grew out of a lesson I learned early, that watching a bill is not the same as managing it.

How do you keep leadership informed?

HOOK Weekly, strategic, end of session, prepped.

Several ways, depending on what they need. Weekly newsletters and status reports, strategic calls when something is moving, end-of-session reports on activity, strategy and results, and briefings that prepare executives before they meet with policymakers. I keep each one short. What changed, what it means and what we need to decide.

You work with a Deputy Governor. What does that relationship look like?

HOOK Raise ours, answer theirs, straight both ways.

It is a working relationship on energy policy. I raise the company’s concerns with the administration, and I respond when they bring issues or requests to us. It works because we are useful to each other and straight with each other.

Your resume says you support the PAC process. What does that mean?

HOOK Working knowledge, objective process, inside the rules.

I want to be clear that I do not run Ameren’s PAC. I know its bylaws, contribution strategy and disclosure requirements well, and I coordinate three or four political fundraising events a year, more than 30 since 2017, all inside the state ethics and campaign finance rules. My view is that contributions follow an objective, documented process tied to policy, never a favor and never a grudge.

How do you keep up with national trends?

HOOK EEI, AGA, EIA, what is coming to Illinois.

Through EEI and the American Gas Association, and by following Energy Information Administration data. I watch federal energy policy, MISO and PJM capacity changes and what other states are doing, because a lot of what lands in Springfield shows up somewhere else first. Then I translate that into what it could mean for our legislative strategy.

The laws and initiatives on your resume

MEMORY HOOK

Four laws, two issues, Resilient Grid.

What exactly was your role on EIMA, FEJA, CEJA and CRGA?

HOOK Support, support, connect, sustain.

I want to be precise, because these were big team efforts. On EIMA in 2011, I did the district work, including an educational tour with legislators and local leaders, and I received the President’s Performance Leadership Award. On FEJA in 2016, I supported passage, including the provisions that preserved the Clinton and Quad Cities nuclear plants and secured infrastructure provisions for us. On CEJA, I connected our internal teams to the legislative effort and kept communication moving. And on CRGA, I maintained key legislative relationships through a multi-year negotiation, and my two assigned issues, data access and thermal networks, were folded into the final law.

Your cover letter mentions data access and thermal energy networks. What happened?

HOOK Already in place, technology limits. Measured until a pilot.

Both came back session after session, and both were assigned to me. I set the internal strategy and kept our team behind one position. On data access, we showed legislators that many of the provisions were already in place and that others ran into real technology limits, and the data retention requirement came down from fifteen years to five. On thermal networks, the original language did not balance what customers would pay against what they would get, so we held to a measured approach until a workable pilot came together. Both ended up in CRGA.

Tell us about Operation Resilient Grid.

HOOK Five plants, 2,092 MW, $45 million, make it local.

It is a multi-track strategy to keep 2,092 MW of natural gas peaking capacity in central and southern Illinois from retiring under CEJA, at a time when data centers are pushing demand up. I lead the legislative workstream. That includes weekly cross-functional coordination, executive briefings, a legislator engagement matrix and coalition trackers for the 2026 to 2027 decision window. To make it local for downstate members, I built a fiscal impact case showing more than $45 million in cumulative property taxes paid to local governments and school districts. The point is that the clean energy transition still needs enough capacity for peak days.

Why would Operation Resilient Grid matter to ComEd?

HOOK Same question in PJM.

Because PJM faces the same question. With load growing, is there enough capacity for peak days while older plants retire? The approach transfers. Build the reliability case, make it local for legislators and bring a coalition that includes labor and local governments.

People and leadership on your resume

MEMORY HOOK

Change, Accountable, Train, Council.

Tell us about your HR work alongside Accenture and IBM.

HOOK Efficiency with people in mind.

In my HR years Ameren went through a lot of change. I worked alongside Accenture and IBM on cost-saving and efficiency initiatives, helped introduce new operating structures and reduce duplication, and guided realignment from recruiting and onboarding to redeployment and separation. I also did compensation mapping and job analysis, worked on two mergers and the first shared services model, and built executive pay and performance models. The lesson was that efficiency only sticks when people understand why and are treated fairly along the way.

At Southwest Benefit Program you managed lawyers, accountants and vendors. How did you hold them accountable?

HOOK Quality, compliance, cost, and the board.

I held every outside firm to the same standard. Clear expectations on service quality, compliance and cost, and regular reviews against them. I negotiated contracts with hospitals, pharmacy suppliers, therapy providers and equipment vendors, managed the budgets and audits, and prepared the board’s materials and recommendations. Working with our attorney, I also helped move the plan out from under heavy Department of Labor oversight. That is the same discipline I would bring to managing contract lobbyists.

Your cover letter says you train new team members. Tell us more.

HOOK Process, ethics, mentoring.

Ameren’s Government Relations team works in a decentralized model, so there is no formal supervisor on each issue. When new people join, I train them on how our department works, bill tracking, expert routing and reporting, and on our ethics expectations. I also guide our contract lobbyists on the issues I lead, and I have mentored people outside the department, including a former Senate staffer who went on to a manager role.

Tell us about the Illinois Utility Business Diversity Council.

HOOK Vice chair, fair and open doors.

I served as Vice Chair from 2016 to 2019. The council brings Illinois utilities together on supplier diversity. As vice chair, I [add one thing you led or the council accomplished]. It reinforced something I believe, that the best way to open doors is a fair, open process every business can use.

Your cover letter

MEMORY HOOK

A third downstate, Chicago ties.

You wrote that Ameren’s territory is about a third of the General Assembly. How do your relationships carry over to ComEd?

HOOK A third downstate, plus Chicago ties, both sides of the aisle.

My relationships run on both sides of the aisle. Legislators from the Ameren Illinois territory make up about a third of the General Assembly, and I have kept them informed on reliability, constituent concerns and storm restoration for years. I have also built relationships with Chicago-area legislators on the many issues that cross both regions. ComEd needs both. City and suburban members, and downstate votes when a bill has to pass statewide.

Part 8

Openers and closers

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. The first 90 seconds and the last 60 are what the panel remembers most.

How to study it.

  1. Learn the opener one paragraph a night. Today, Roots, GR, How I lead, Ready.
  2. Add a new paragraph only when the last one is smooth.
  3. Record yourself on your phone once a week and listen back one time.

Watch for.

  • Rushing. Pause between paragraphs. Silence sounds confident.
  • Saying too much on why now. Keep family needs general and stop there.

Mindset. You are telling your story, not reciting a speech. If a word slips, say the next idea in plain words and keep going.

Say it back. Say the five labels, then the whole opener in about 90 seconds.

Say these the way you would tell your story over lunch to another executive. The beats matter more than the exact words.

Tell me about yourself

MEMORY HOOK

Today, Roots, GR, How I lead, Ready. Walk your career in order, then say how you lead and why ComEd.

About 90 seconds. Each paragraph has one job.

TODAY Thank you for having me. Today I’m a Senior Government Relations Representative at Ameren Illinois. I’ve been in Government Relations for eighteen years, and I’m my department’s lead on data center, battery storage and decarbonization legislation.

ROOTS I started on the people and business side. I ran a union health and welfare plan with a staff of seven and a board of trustees. Then I joined Ameren in HR, where I worked on two mergers, the company’s first shared services model, consolidation and streamlining, and executive pay and performance modeling. That’s where I learned how a company really runs, and how to lead people through change.

GR In 2008 I moved to Government Relations. My job is to bring legal, regulatory, operations and our executives to one company position, and then win support for it in Springfield. A recent example is thermal energy networks. A bill we couldn’t support in 2025 became a workable part of CRGA.

HOW I LEAD The way I lead comes down to four things. No surprises for the executives. One voice for the company. Doing it the right way, every time. And a team that gets stronger because I’m part of it.

READY I’m ready to lead with the title now, and ComEd is where I want to do it.

WHY THIS VERSION WORKS

  • It follows your career in order, so it is easy for you to remember and easy for the panel to follow.

  • Each paragraph does one job. Where you are today, where you came from, what you do, how you lead, why ComEd.

  • It states your leadership thread in plain words, so the panel hears it before any story.

  • It answers the supervision question early, with your staff of seven and your HR work through two mergers.

Why ComEd, and why leave Ameren?

MEMORY HOOK

Thanks, Seats, Scale, Season. Grateful to Ameren, only so many seats, ComEd’s scale and issues, the right season of life.

I have had a great run at Ameren and I am grateful for it. Honestly, there are only so many director seats in a GR department, and ComEd is a company I have wanted to work for for years. It is the largest utility in the state, and the issues it faces, data centers, affordability and CRGA, are the ones I work on every day. My kids are grown, so moving to Chicago and spending the weeks in Springfield and the long nights during storms is not a hard ask for me now.

Follow-up if asked, why now?

MEMORY HOOK

Family first then. Behind me now. Ready to lead.

I have enjoyed my time at Ameren, and I want to say that first. Earlier in my career I made a deliberate choice. My family needed me close, and I chose work that let me be there for them. I was not chasing a title then. I wanted to be very good at the work and present at home. It was the right call, and I would make it again.

That season is behind me now. I am an empty nester, my time and energy are my own, and I am ready for what this job asks, including weeks in Springfield and long nights during storms. When I took a hard look at what I want from this next chapter, the answer was to lead. ComEd has been on my short list for years, so when this role opened, I did not have to think long.

If they ask what changed

I had a child who needed more of me than most, and parents who needed care. My child is grown and my parents have passed. Those were the right priorities at the time, and they taught me a lot about patience and planning.

If they ask why you did not move into leadership sooner

Two honest reasons. I chose roles that fit what my family needed from me, and Government Relations is a small function where leadership seats rarely open. What grew in that time was my scope. I became my department’s lead on data center, storage and decarbonization bills and sat at the table with senior leaders on the company’s biggest issues.

KEEP IT PRIVATE

You never need to share health, medical, marriage or other personal details. Panels are not supposed to ask, and volunteering them can plant a doubt that was not there. "My family needed me close" is complete and honest. Say it once, calmly, and move to why you are ready now.

What are your weaknesses?

MEMORY HOOK

Headline first. Deadline first. Detail is fixed by leading with the answer. Impatience is fixed by setting the deadline up front.

I tend to give too much detail. I come from a world where leaving something out can hurt you, so my instinct is to cover everything. I have learned to lead with the answer and the decision we need, and keep the detail ready for whoever wants it. With executives that means a one-page brief with the backup behind it.

I can also get impatient pushing people to a position. In GR the clock runs on the legislature’s schedule, not ours. What I have learned is to set the deadline up front and explain why, so people see it is the session calendar driving it and not me.

The posting asks for five years of supervision. Tell us about yours.

This is the question most likely to test you, because you have no direct reports today. Answer it with confidence.

MEMORY HOOK

Seven, seven, five, plus the hard kind. A team of seven for seven years, five years in HR, and leading people who do not report to you.

I ran the staff at Southwest Benefit Program for seven years. That was a team of seven covering accounting, payroll, claims and union liaison, plus our outside counsel and accountants, and I reported to a board of trustees. At Ameren I spent five years in HR advising managers on discipline, terminations, succession and labor relations, and I worked on two merger integrations, from benefits rollout and aligning jobs and people to onboarding. So I know the people side of supervision from the inside. In Government Relations our team works in a decentralized model, so I train new team members on our processes and ethics expectations, guide contract lobbyists on my issues and lead cross-functional teams that do not report to me, which in a lot of ways is harder. Having a GR team on my own org chart is exactly the part of this job I am ready for.

If asked about leading change or your HR background

MEMORY HOOK

Two mergers, shared services, pay models. People need the why.

Before Government Relations, I spent five years in Ameren’s HR group during a period of real change. I worked on two mergers from the people side, rolling out employee benefits, aligning jobs and people, organizational development and onboarding. I worked on streamlining and consolidation, including the company’s first shared services model. And I built executive pay and performance models and shared them with leadership.

What I learned is that change works when people understand why, know what is expected of them and see their leaders follow through. That carries straight into Government Relations, because getting a whole company to one position is change management too.

What would you do in your first 90 days?

MEMORY HOOK

Listen, Map, Plan. Thirty, sixty, ninety.

First 30 days, listen. I would meet each person on the team one on one, and meet the executive team, regulatory, legal and the business leaders. I would get to know the contract lobbyists and where each relationship stands, and I would sit down with compliance early so I know exactly how ComEd does things.

Days 30 to 60, map the session. What is coming on CRGA implementation, data centers and affordability, which members and staff matter most, and where we are exposed.

By day 90, bring a plan. Priorities for the session, a clear role for each person on the team, a simple bill tracking and expert review process, and a regular reporting rhythm so nobody on the executive team is ever surprised.

Questions to ask the panel

MEMORY HOOK

Success, Speed, Magic wand. Ask them in this order.

Ask What you learn
Success. What does success look like in this role? If we are sitting together a year from now, what would I have done to earn a strong review? Their real priorities and how they will measure you.
Speed. How does your team like to collaborate, especially when things move fast or priorities shift? The leadership style and who makes decisions under pressure.
Magic wand. If you could wave a magic wand, what is the one challenge your team faces today that you would solve overnight? The real pain point. If it fits, connect it to one of your stories in a sentence.
Backup. Coming out of CRGA and the grid plan, where do you expect the next big legislative fight to be? Use it if one of the first three was already answered.

Closing statement

MEMORY HOOK

Know it, Lead it, Grow it, Ask for it. Springfield and the business, lead with no surprises, one voice and the right way, a stronger team, then ask for the job.

About 60 seconds.

Thank you. I’ve enjoyed this conversation.

I’d like to leave you with three things. First, I know Springfield, and I know the business behind the policy. I’ve spent eighteen years making sure what we say in the Capitol matches what the company can actually deliver.

Second, I’d lead this team the way I’ve always worked. No surprises for the executive team, one voice for the company, and the right way, every time.

Third, I care about developing people. I’d want this team to be stronger because I’m on it.

I’m ready for this, and I’d very much like the chance to do it at ComEd.

WHAT CHANGED FROM YOUR DRAFT

  • It asks for the job in plain words at the end.

  • It touches your leadership thread once, lightly, in the second point, so it echoes your opening without repeating it.

  • "Doing it the right way every time" signals integrity to a ComEd panel without mentioning the history.

  • It trades general claims like "sound political judgment" and "established relationships" for things you can show.
