Part 9

Eleven anchor stories

✦Coach’s corner

Why this matters. These eleven stories are the heart of the interview. Together they can answer almost any behavioral question.

How to study it.

  1. Two stories a session, never more.
  2. Learn the five-word chain first, then the turning point, then tell it out loud.
  3. Next session, retell the last two before you add new ones.

Watch for.

  • Saying we for everything. Say what you did, then credit the team.
  • Ending on the result. End on what it says about how you lead.

Mindset. A real story you can defend beats a polished one you cannot. Yours are real.

Say it back. For each story you have learned, give the room, the chain and the last line.

Each story fits in about two minutes. The leadership point is what you say last. The follow-ups are where panels separate real stories from rehearsed ones, so practice those as much as the main answer.

Brackets mark the few spots where only you have the fact. Fill them before you rehearse.

HOW TO LEARN EACH STORY IN FIVE MINUTES

  1. Read the five-word STAR chain and picture the room.

  2. Read the full answer once, out loud.

  3. Cover the page and tell it from the chain alone.

  4. Uncover, check what you dropped, and tell it again.

  5. Answer one follow-up cold.

Story 1 Thermal energy networks to CRGA

✦Coach’s note

This is your lead story. Be exact about your role. You set the internal strategy, and colleagues led the coalition work. The turning point is 2025, when saying no would not hold, so you offered a workable path. Say it slowly. It is your best proof.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about one of the most significant public-policy accomplishments of your career. What was your personal contribution?

Also asked as

  • Tell me about a time you developed a government affairs strategy around a major legislative or regulatory issue.

  • Describe a time you had to reposition a proposal because the political environment changed.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Sweeping decarb bill Set the strategy Split it, two tracks, pilot path Tabled, then CRGA Include all, offer a path
ROOM 1 FRONT PORCH A round table sits on your porch with gas pipes for legs. A small pilot light burns on top of a law book stamped CRGA.
Best for Most significant accomplishment, developing a GR strategy, coalition work, repositioning when politics shift, short-term win versus long-term objective
Turning point A sweeping bill with real momentum. Saying no would not hold, so we offered a workable path.
Remember it as Don’t just oppose. Bring everyone in early, then offer a workable path.

THE ANSWER

Situation In 2025, thermal energy networks legislation came in as part of a bigger package of Illinois decarbonization bills. On paper it was about thermal networks. In practice it reached into gas line extensions, the obligation to serve, fixed charges, low-income programs and the long-term role of the gas system.

Task The issue was assigned to me. My job was to set the company's strategy and get us to a position leadership could stand behind.

Action I started inside. I brought in the right subject matter experts and our gas leadership, and we broke a very long bill into separate questions. For each provision we asked what it does, what it means for customers, what it means for operations, whether it is technically workable, and if we object, what we would offer instead.

Externally we ran two tracks. We stayed aligned with the other Illinois utilities and the Illinois Energy Association, and we put our contract lobbyists where their relationships were strongest. At the same time we kept talking with the sponsor and the environmental groups, not only our usual allies.

The hard part was momentum. Decarbonization had real support, so a flat no was not going to hold. We agreed with the goal and showed where affordability, feasibility and the effect on the electric system had not been worked out. Then we offered a path. Study it, pilot it, prove the customer value, and then scale it.

Result The bill was tabled in 2025. A workable version of the policy then became law as part of CRGA. We did not stop the idea. We helped turn it into something that can actually be built and paid for, and we kept good relationships with the people on the other side of the table.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

I bring the right people in before we take a position. The right experts, executives and outside voices come in early, and our own people understand why a constructive path protects the company better than opposition does. That is the kind of judgment a director has to bring to the executive team.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Be exact about your role. You set the internal strategy. Colleagues led the coalition work, so say "we" for that track and give them credit if asked.

  • Never call the environmental groups opponents. Say "the other side of the table" or "stakeholders who wanted to move faster."

  • ComEd is implementing CRGA now. Expect a follow-up on what the law means for them.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

What was the hardest part?

Honestly, it was inside the company. The natural reaction was to oppose it. I had to show our leaders that the goal had real momentum and that a flat no would cost us the room. Once they saw that, we could put our energy into shaping it instead of fighting it.

What ended up in CRGA, and do you count that as a win?

What passed was a pilot approach, with financing available through the Illinois Finance Authority. Yes, I count it as a win. What passed is something a utility can implement and customers can afford, and it reflects the pilot-first approach we argued for.

Who were the key decision makers?

The sponsor, the House Energy and Environment Committee, leadership, the progressive caucus, legislators in our territory and the environmental organizations. Then I matched each one with the most credible messenger, whether that was one of our experts, an executive, a contract lobbyist or the industry association.

How did you measure success?

Four things. Problem provisions did not move before they were ready. Our concerns became part of the real policy conversation. Key relationships held up. And the issue moved toward something that could be implemented. Sometimes success is changing the direction so everyone ends up with better choices.

Story 2 The senator's vendor list

✦Coach’s note

Tell it calmly and plainly. The point is the process, not you as the hero. Never name the senator, and let the panel connect it to ComEd's history on their own.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time political pressure conflicted with the company's legal, ethical or compliance obligations.

Also asked as

  • Describe a situation where a stakeholder asked for something the company could not appropriately provide.

  • How do you make sure lobbyists and consultants stay inside the company's compliance rules?

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Senator’s list and a threat Rules and the relationship No promise, the process, report up Pressure stopped Same rules for all
ROOM 2 FRONT DOOR A former senator wedges a list in your front door. You point to a sign on the door that reads Same Door for Every Vendor, then call your boss.
Best for Ethics and compliance, political pressure, a request the company could not grant, keeping lobbyists and consultants aligned with the rules
Turning point A former senator wanted his list of businesses to get contracts, with a threat attached.
Remember it as Same rules for every vendor, and leadership hears it from me first.

THE ANSWER

Situation A former state senator handed me a list of minority-owned businesses and told me he wanted them to get contracts with the company. He made it clear that if we did not, he would make things difficult for us.

Task I had to protect the company and keep the relationship workable without bending the rules. I also had to handle it so it never sounded like we were against supplier diversity, because we were not.

Action I made no promises in the room. I told him the company supports diverse suppliers and has a vendor application and review process that every business goes through, and that I would make sure the businesses on his list knew how to use it.

Then I went to my leadership and reported exactly what was said, including the threat. I did not try to manage it on my own. When he pressed again, he got the same answer. We would not go around our process for anyone.

Result The businesses were pointed to the same front door as every other vendor, and the pressure stopped. Leadership heard about it from me first, not from someone else, so nobody was caught off guard.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Integrity in this job is mostly about process. Know the rules, apply them the same way for everyone, report up early, and you never have to remember what you told someone. As a director I would expect the same from every person and every contract lobbyist on the team.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Do not name the senator.

  • Do not draw the line to ComEd's history yourself. The panel will make that connection on their own.

  • Tell it plainly. The point is the process, not you being the hero.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

What would you do if a legislator asked ComEd for something like that?

Exactly the same thing. Be respectful, point them to the process, and tell my leadership and compliance that day. I would also make sure the whole team is trained so any one of us would give the same answer.

How do you keep lobbyists and consultants in line with compliance?

Everyone works from the same rules. We follow the state ethics rules and report out, a third-party auditor follows up twice a year, legal reinforces it, and our company president made compliance non-negotiable. I would hold contract lobbyists to the same standard and I would check, not assume.

Was there a cost to saying no?

There is always some risk when you tell a powerful person no. I managed it by keeping leadership informed and keeping my tone respectful. The cost of bending the rules would have been far higher.

Story 3 EIMA

✦Coach’s note

Use EIMA to show leading without authority, not as your headline. If the history comes up, give one calm answer and move on.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you led a major initiative involving people who did not report to you.

Also asked as

  • How have you explained the link between grid investment, reliability and customer bills to policymakers?

  • Tell me about a time you aligned several internal departments around one government affairs position.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
First big test, 2011 Territory support Districts, tour, give them a reason Veto overridden, 2013 award Win inside first
ROOM 3 LIVING ROOM A 2011 tour bus is parked in your living room, packed with legislators. A 2013 award plaque hangs over the fireplace.
Best for Leading without authority, aligning internal functions, explaining grid investment and customer bills, an early-career test
Turning point Three years into lobbying, a major bill that meant higher bills, and help I needed from people who did not report to me.
Remember it as Win support inside the company before asking legislators for theirs.

THE ANSWER

Situation I had been lobbying about three years when the Energy Infrastructure Modernization Act came in. It was my first big test.

Task On the Ameren Illinois side, my job was to build support among the legislators in our service territory and make sure what we told them was backed by real information from across the company.

Action I spent a lot of time in the districts explaining why the grid needed the investment, what customers would get from it, and the hard part, that investment shows up on bills. I did not dodge that. I tied the cost to reliability and to our ability to serve customers for the long haul. I also ran an educational tour across our territory with district legislators and local officials so they could see the system for themselves.

Inside the company, I needed help from technical, customer, regulatory and communications people who did not report to me. I learned to give them a reason to care. Instead of saying GR needs this, I told them what legislators were asking and how the outcome would affect their part of the business.

At one point a misunderstanding over House sponsorship reached the company president. I slowed it down, got the facts straight, confirmed the strategy, and worked directly with the legislator to fix it without losing his support.

Result EIMA became law in October 2011 when the General Assembly overrode the governor's veto, and in 2013 I received the President's Performance Leadership Award for my part. It is also where I learned that big outcomes are usually won inside the company before they are won outside.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

I lead across functions by making the work matter to them. I am upfront about tradeoffs with legislators, and when something goes sideways I slow it down, get the facts, and repair it in person.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Use EIMA for leading without authority, not as your headline accomplishment. Thermal energy networks to CRGA is your lead.

  • Stay calm and brief if the history comes up. One answer, then move on.

  • Do not name the legislator in the sponsorship story.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

EIMA is tied to ComEd's history. What did you see?

My work was on the Ameren Illinois side, in our districts, educating legislators and local leaders. I had no part in and no view into what came out later about ComEd. What it taught everyone in this industry, me included, is that how you win matters as much as whether you win. Every relationship I have built has been built in the open and inside the rules, and that is how I would lead here.

How did you handle the rate question with legislators?

Directly. Yes, this investment will be on bills, and here is what you and your constituents get for it. Legislators trust you more when you do not pretend there is no cost.

What did the sponsorship mix-up teach you?

Do not let an internal misunderstanding become an external problem. Get the facts, confirm what strategy is authorized, and fix the relationship personally.

Story 4 Late-session broadband language

✦Coach’s note

The lesson is no surprises. Frame it as fairness for rural customers, never as utility against co-op. Be ready to link it to Story 5 in one sentence.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a legislative crisis where you had very little time to act.

Also asked as

  • Describe a time legislative language surfaced without adequate review. How did you organize the company's response?

  • Tell me about a time you had to protect the company from an unfavorable precedent.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Late language, IOUs shut out Hours to respond Two tracks, three questions, policy case Language died, bill narrowed Speed with a plan
ROOM 4 KITCHEN A fiber cable boils over on the stove. The oven timer reads hours, not days. Three sticky notes on the fridge say What happens, Smallest fix, Who can change it.
Best for Crisis with little time, language that skipped review, unfavorable precedent, briefing executives under pressure, managing several risks at once
Turning point Late in session, language that would have shut investor-owned utilities out of broadband use of their own easements.
Remember it as In a crisis, ask three things. What happens, what’s the smallest fix, who can make it.

THE ANSWER

Situation Late in session, new language showed up in a broadband bill. It would have limited the use of existing electric easements for broadband to electric co-ops and their territories, and left investor-owned utilities out. That mattered to us. Ameren Illinois serves a lot of rural communities where broadband is hard to reach, and our infrastructure and fiber could help.

Task The language had not been through any normal review, and we had hours, not days. I had to organize our response.

Action First, I did not let the urgency turn into chaos. I set up two tracks. Legal and our technical people worked out what the language actually did, what it meant for customers and operations, and the smallest fix. Government Relations confirmed what the sponsor intended, where the bill stood procedurally, and who could actually change it.

I gave leadership a heads-up right away with what we knew, what we did not know, what was at stake, and when I would be back with a recommendation. And I boiled the work down to three questions. What happens if this passes? What is the smallest fix? Who can make it before the window closes?

Then we turned the technical concern into a policy argument. If Illinois wants broadband in underserved areas, access should not depend on which kind of utility serves the town. We lined up our message, drafted corrective language and kept fallback options ready.

Result The language did not move. The sponsor narrowed the bill to focus on rural communities served by municipal and cooperative utilities, so the broad version that would have set the precedent never became law.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

In a crisis my job is to turn confusion into a few clear decisions and make sure each group works on the part it owns. Legal takes the legal question, operations the operational one, GR the politics, and executives make the calls only they can make. Speed matters, but organized speed matters more.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Do not criticize the co-ops. Frame it as fairness for rural customers, not utility against utility.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

How did you decide what to tell leadership, and when?

Early and short. What we know, what we do not, the exposure, and when I will be back. Executives can handle bad news. What they cannot handle is a surprise.

What if the language had kept moving?

We had a narrower amendment and fallback language ready, and we knew who could carry it. The minimum fix was always on the table so the sponsor had an easy way to say yes.

Story 5 Engaging early on broadband

✦Coach’s note

Show patience and judgment. You raised real concerns without a company position yet. The result to say is that the sponsor narrowed the bill to rural communities served by municipal and co-op utilities.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you made an important Government Relations decision without all the information you wanted.

Also asked as

  • Describe a time you faced pressure to take a position before the technical or regulatory analysis was complete.

  • Tell me about a time you had to set decision rights on a fast-moving issue.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Drafts, no position Engage or wait Principles, guardrails, triggers Influence kept, ready to move At the table, not endorsing
ROOM 5 DINING ROOM Your seat at the table has a place card that reads Not Endorsing, and a small guardrail fence circles your plate.
Best for Deciding without all the information, pressure to take a position before analysis is complete, decision rights
Turning point Real concerns with the drafts, but no authorized company position yet.
Remember it as Being at the table is not the same as supporting the bill.

THE ANSWER

Situation A broadband proposal was still developing. We had reviewed several drafts and had real concerns, but senior leadership had not yet authorized a company position. If we waited for perfect information we could lose our influence. If we jumped in too hard, it could look like support or opposition leadership had not approved.

Task I had to recommend whether and how we should engage.

Action I separated the decision to engage from the decision to support. I weighed what was at stake, the timing, how much we could influence it, how reversible each choice was, and who had the authority to decide. I recommended engaging on principles rather than taking a formal position on incomplete language.

Inside the company I set guardrails. What we could support, what needed technical review, what we could not accept, and what had to go to executives. Outside, I was clear that being at the table did not mean we supported language we had not reviewed. I also set triggers to reassess, such as new drafts, committee timing, a sponsor change or the administration getting involved.

Result We kept our influence on the proposal while leadership kept the final call. When the language did change, we already knew the issue and the players and were ready to respond.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Incomplete information is not a reason to freeze or to guess. A leader works out which decision has to be made now. Sometimes the right answer is that we know enough to take this step, not the next one, and here is what will make us look again.

WATCH-OUTS

  • This pairs with Story 4. If you tell one, be ready to connect them in a sentence.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

How did you keep the company from looking like it endorsed the bill?

I said it plainly every time. We are here to understand and to share our concerns, and we have not taken a position. Then I made sure our contract lobbyists said exactly the same thing.

What would have made you change course?

The triggers we set. A new draft, a committee date, a change in sponsor or the administration weighing in. Any one of those sent us back to leadership.

Story 6 The bill I did not route

✦Coach’s note

Own the miss in one sentence. Spend most of your time on the fix, the tracker and the SME database. Keep it early in your career and do not name the bill.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you did not achieve the policy outcome you wanted.

Also asked as

  • Tell me about a strategy that did not produce the outcome you expected. What did you misjudge, and what did you change?

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Low-risk bill, leaned on industry No position when it moved Owned it, built the tracker Tracker and SME database Monitoring is not managing
ROOM 6 HALLWAY A bill slides down the hallway past a closed door marked Experts. Now a big weekly calendar hangs on the wall.
Best for A policy effort that did not go the way you wanted, a strategy you misjudged, building a process
Turning point I treated a bill as low risk, leaned on the industry, and could not give leadership a position when it moved.
Remember it as Watching a bill is not managing it. Every bill goes to the experts.

THE ANSWER

Situation Early in my career I was assigned a bill that looked like it had little to do with us. I knew the broader industry was engaged, so I decided on my own to follow the industry process instead of running the bill through our internal review. That was a mistake.

Task When the bill moved out of committee, leadership asked where Ameren stood, and I had to own the fact that I could not give them a defensible answer.

Action I had not done the baseline work with our subject matter experts. I had confused monitoring an issue with managing it, and by the time I saw the difference we had lost time and options. I owned that with leadership.

Then I changed how I work. I built a legislative tracker and started routing every assigned bill to the right experts, no matter how relevant I thought it was. I documented their feedback and our position, followed up when responses were missing, and checked whether the feedback was real or just a box being checked.

Result That process became how I work to this day. Every assigned bill goes on a weekly tracker, and I have since built a subject matter expert database that routes a bill or an issue to the right leader or team quickly. A miss on one bill turned into a system the department can use.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

I own my misses out loud and then fix the process, not just the instance. Industry coordination is valuable, but the company's accountability cannot be handed off. Early review keeps every option open, whether that is to educate, amend, support, oppose or wait.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Keep it early in your career. Do not name the bill.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

What did you tell leadership in the moment?

The truth. I did not have a vetted position, here is why, and here is when I will have one. Then I delivered it.

How do you keep a process like that from becoming busywork?

I check the quality of the answers, not just whether they came back. If the feedback is thin, I go back and ask the harder question.

Story 7 Leave no man behind

✦Coach’s note

This is a story about growth. Speak of the president with respect. His advice changed how you lead, so let the panel feel that.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you failed.

Also asked as

  • Tell me about feedback that changed the way you work.

  • How have you created consistency across a team whose members manage different relationships?

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Lone results The president’s feedback Listened, debriefs, shared relationships Team shared more Team stronger, not just me
ROOM 7 STAIRCASE You reach the top of the stairs alone. The president is waiting and points back down. You go back and bring the team up with you.
Best for A personal failure, feedback you received, teamwork, building consistency across a team
Turning point I was producing results on my own and the company president told me that was not enough.
Remember it as My job is to make the whole team stronger, not just me.

THE ANSWER

Situation Early in my lobbying career I became very independent. I traveled the service territory, built legislative relationships, learned the business and got results, so I thought I was doing everything right. My blind spot was that I treated what I knew and who I knew as my own, instead of something that should make the whole department stronger.

Task The company president called me into his office, shared some of his own career, and told me to leave no man behind. He said the job was not a solo adventure, and being of service to legislators was not enough. I also had to be of service to my peers. It was hard to hear, and he was right.

Action I sat down with a colleague and mentor who felt I was not acting as a team player, and I listened to how my behavior was landing with the team. Then I changed how I worked. I started sending written debriefs after meetings, sharing political context in team meetings, bringing colleagues into my relationships, and bringing what I learned about the business back to the group.

Result The team started sharing more with each other too. We were better informed and better prepared, and I was a better colleague.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Being a strong individual and being a leader are different things. A strong individual collects knowledge, relationships and influence. A leader turns those into something the whole team can use. Today I ask whether the team is better informed and better connected because of how I work.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Speak of the president with respect. The story honors his advice.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

How did you feel when you heard that?

Embarrassed at first. Then grateful, because he cared enough to tell me early.

How would you build that sharing habit on a team you lead?

Make it routine. Short written debriefs, a standing time in team meetings for political intelligence, and making sure relationships are shared so no member of the legislature depends on one person.

Story 8 The SME and the legislator

✦Coach’s note

Show that you prepare experts and protect relationships. Stay neutral about both people, and never name them.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Describe a situation where you had to hold someone accountable while maintaining the relationship.

Also asked as

  • Tell me about a time you had to manage a difficult person.

  • Tell me about a time you corrected someone more senior than you.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Expert loses his cool Save the meeting, coach him Step in, follow up, private talk Prep standard, kept the expert Value the expert, fix behavior
ROOM 8 DEN An expert in a lab coat argues with a legislator. You step between them holding two cards, one says Value and one says Behavior.
Best for Holding someone accountable while keeping the relationship, leading a difficult person, holding someone senior to account
Turning point A company director I brought into a legislative meeting took a challenge personally and the meeting turned tense.
Remember it as Value the expert, correct the behavior.

THE ANSWER

Situation I brought a senior subject matter expert, a company director, into a meeting with a legislator to explain a technical issue. The legislator challenged our position, the expert took it personally, his tone got sharp, and the meeting started to turn adversarial.

Task I had to protect the relationship with the legislator in the moment, and then hold a senior colleague accountable without losing him as a resource.

Action I stepped in before it did lasting damage. I acknowledged the legislator's concern, clarified where we actually disagreed, and moved the conversation to the information we still needed to work through. Afterward I followed up with the legislator, confirmed I understood his concern, and committed to keep working on it.

Then I met privately with the expert. I told him his expertise was exactly why I needed him in the room, and I was just as clear that the way he handled it would not work in a legislative setting. We were not there to win an argument. We were there to explain consequences, understand the concern and set up the next conversation. Lobbying is a long campaign, not one meeting.

Result He understood that the Capitol works differently from an internal business debate. From then on I prepared every non-GR colleague before legislative meetings on the goal, their role, the audience, likely friction, the handoffs and when to wrap up. Those meetings went better, and he stayed a strong resource for us.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Accountability can protect a relationship when it is private, specific, tied to impact and followed by a clear standard. My HR background helps here. Address it quickly, describe the behavior and its effect, listen, agree on what comes next, and follow up.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Do not name the expert or the legislator.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

He outranked you. How did you handle that?

I respected his role and his expertise, and I was clear about mine. He owns the technical answer. GR owns the advocacy setting. Framed that way, it was not personal.

How would you handle it if it happened again with the same person?

Same approach, a shorter fuse. A direct conversation, and if it continued, I would involve his leader and adjust who represents us in front of legislators.

Story 9 Advising leadership to stay engaged

✦Coach’s note

This shows courage to advise upward, with a recommendation attached. Say senior leadership, not a title, and keep the PAC out of it unless asked.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Give me an example of when you had to tell senior leadership something it did not want to hear.

Also asked as

  • Describe a time internal leaders disagreed about how to handle a legislator or issue. How did you help them decide?

  • Tell me about a time you chose a long-term relationship over a short-term reaction.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Heated meeting, pull back Candid advice Facts, voting record, process, reset Stayed engaged Votes and process
ROOM 9 HOME OFFICE A scale sits on your desk. One side holds a thick voting record, the other a small storm cloud. The record wins.
Best for Telling senior leadership something it did not want to hear, internal disagreement, short-term reaction versus long-term relationship
Turning point After a heated meeting, leadership was ready to step back from a legislator whose votes we needed.
Remember it as Decide on the voting record and our process, not on how one meeting felt.

THE ANSWER

Situation A legislator challenged our company often, mostly on affordability and supplier diversity. After a working group meeting I did not attend got heated, senior leadership was ready to step back from him.

Task I had to give candid advice that ran against where leadership was leaning.

Action I started by understanding what had happened in that meeting. Then I went to the record. His voting record showed steady support on several of our major priorities. I said plainly that how one meeting felt could not drive our legislative strategy, and that there would be moments when every vote counted. I also said any decisions about political support had to stay inside our established, objective process, the same as always.

I recommended a reset. Treat his concerns as legitimate even where we disagreed with his answers, keep engaging on the facts, and keep the institutional relationship separate from any personal friction.

Result Leadership was not thrilled at first, but agreed that stepping back created more risk than it solved. We kept a working relationship with him.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Courage with senior leaders is not confrontation. It is separating emotion from evidence, making the consequences clear and recommending what serves the company over the long run. Government Relations manages risk inside the company as well as outside.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Say "senior leadership," not a title. Do not describe anyone's temper or which members leadership liked better.

  • Keep the PAC out of this story unless asked. If asked, the answer is that contributions follow an objective, documented process.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

How did you deliver that advice?

Privately, respectfully, and with the facts in front of us. I acknowledged the frustration first. People hear hard advice better when they feel heard.

What would you have done if leadership had decided to pull back anyway?

Carried out the decision, kept the door open with the legislator at a staff level, and brought it back up when the facts gave us a reason to.

Story 10 Mentoring a finalist we did not hire

✦Coach’s note

A warm story, so keep it short. Say a former Senate staffer, give her the credit, and end on growing talent wherever you find it.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you mentored or developed someone and helped them reach their professional goals.

Also asked as

  • What is your philosophy on developing people?

  • Tell me about a government affairs professional you developed.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Finalist not hired Mentor for the long run Quarterly talks, org savvy, visibility New role, then manager Grow talent anywhere
ROOM 10 GARAGE You hold a ladder steady while a former Senate staffer climbs up to a sign that reads Manager.
Best for Developing someone, coaching, succession, leading outside your reporting line
Turning point A strong finalist was not selected and asked me for feedback, which turned into mentoring.
Remember it as Develop talent wherever you find it, even outside your own team.

THE ANSWER

Situation A while back I sat on the interview panel for an opening in our Government Relations department. One of the finalists was a former Senate staffer who had joined Ameren. She was not selected, but her background, ability and ambition stood out to me.

Task After the process she reached out for feedback, and that turned into her asking me to mentor her. My goal was not just to help her find another job. It was to help her see where her skills could take her and position herself for the long run.

Action We met every quarter. We talked about her goals, her strengths, where she needed to grow and how that lined up with what the company needed. I helped her understand how the organization works, how leadership looks at talent, why relationships across departments matter and where her legislative experience could add value. I also pushed her to think beyond her current lane and be more deliberate about her visibility and her career choices.

Result Within about a year another opportunity opened up and she earned it. More recently she was promoted into a manager role. The credit is hers. I am glad I had a small part in it.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Developing people is not limited to the people who report to you. Good leaders notice talent across the company and help it grow, and the whole organization benefits. One of the ways I measure myself is the talent I leave behind.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Do not use her name in the interview. Say "a former Senate staffer."

  • Give her the credit for earning both positions.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

What is your philosophy on developing people?

It starts with understanding what each person wants, because not everyone has the same goals. From there my job is candid feedback, real exposure, a stretch assignment and helping them see how their work fits the bigger picture. If the people around me are getting more capable and more confident, I am doing my job.

Have you developed people who reported to you?

Yes. At Southwest Benefit Program I had a staff of seven, and today I train new Government Relations team members on our processes and ethics expectations. [Add one person you helped grow there and what changed for them.] And in my HR years I advised leaders on succession planning, so I know how to build a bench deliberately.

How would you develop the team here?

One-on-ones focused on each person's goals, a portfolio for each person they truly own, debriefs after big meetings, and making sure their good work is seen by the executive team.

Story 11 Utility data access

✦Coach’s note

This is your backup accomplishment. Use it if they already heard Story 1. Say CRGA, not CEJA. Retention went from 15 years to 5.

INTERVIEW QUESTION

Tell me about a time you successfully changed or shaped legislative language.

Also asked as

  • Describe a situation where you had to decide whether an issue belonged in statute or at the ICC.

  • Give me an example of how you preserved regulatory flexibility while negotiating legislation.

S Situation T Task A Action R Result L Leadership
Data need, no framework Set the internal strategy Experts, principles, statute or ICC Fifteen to five, into CRGA Principles in law, details at ICC
ROOM 11 BACKYARD A fence marked Statute surrounds the garden. The ICC is the gardener tending the plants inside.
Best for Backup accomplishment, changing legislative language, statute versus ICC, keeping regulatory flexibility
Turning point A proposal that came back every session, with provisions already in place and others the technology could not support.
Remember it as Principles go in the law. Technical details go to the ICC.

THE ANSWER

Situation Utility data access legislation came back session after session. Some versions would have created new rules for customer data access and retention, including keeping customer data for fifteen years. A poorly written mandate could have created cost, privacy and operational problems.

Task The proposal was assigned to me. I set the company’s internal strategy and kept our team behind one position.

Action I brought together legal, regulatory, operations, customer and technical experts to define the problem and agree on principles. Then we sorted what truly needed to be in statute from the details that belonged at the ICC.

With sponsors and legislators, we showed that many of the proposed provisions were already in place and that others ran into real technology limits. That gave policymakers something workable instead of an objection.

Result The retention requirement came down from fifteen years to five, and a workable version was folded into CRGA. My part was the foundation under the advocacy. The problem definition, the principles, one company position and the line between statute and regulation.

HOW THIS SHOWS LEADERSHIP

Good policy work starts with defining the problem before arguing a position. Putting the right details in the right venue protects customers and keeps the company flexible as things change.

WATCH-OUTS

  • Use this as your backup if the panel has already heard Story 1 or wants a second accomplishment.

LIKELY FOLLOW-UPS

Who led the outside work?

Colleagues led the broader coalition work. I set the strategy, kept our team behind one position and advocated directly with sponsors and legislators. I am glad to give them credit for their part.

Why leave the details to the ICC?

Because technology and customer needs change faster than statute. The law should set the protections and the goal. The ICC can update the details with a full record.
